from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Two blocks on a frictionless surface.", "Small block sits between wall and large block.", "Elastic collisions conserve energy and momentum.", "Collisions begin as the large block approaches.", "This creates a rapid ping-pong effect."]
        self.setup_layout("The Setup: A Curious Mechanical System", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        block1 = Square(side_length=0.8, color=BLUE_B).set_fill(opacity=0.7)
        block2 = Rectangle(width=1.6, height=0.8, color=GREEN_B).set_fill(opacity=0.7)
        self.place_at_grid(block1, "B2")
        self.place_at_grid(block2, "B4")
        self.play(FadeIn(block1), FadeIn(block2))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        wall = Line(start=self.grid["A1"]+DOWN*0.5, end=self.grid["F1"]+UP*0.5, color=WHITE, stroke_width=8)
        self.add(wall)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        energy_label = MathTex("E_{total}", "=", "const").scale(0.8).next_to(block2, UP)
        self.play(Write(energy_label))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.play(block2.animate.move_to(block1.get_right() + RIGHT * 0.4))
        collision_pt = Dot(point=block1.get_right(), color=RED)
        self.play(Flash(collision_pt))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.play(FadeOut(block1), FadeOut(block2), FadeOut(energy_label), FadeOut(wall))

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite Knowledge: Conservation Laws", [
            "Elastic collisions preserve total energy.",
            "Both kinetic energy and momentum are conserved.",
            "Blocks trade velocities based on mass ratios."

        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===

        self.play(
            Indicate(conservation_group, color="#FFFF00"),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFFF00")

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Collisions trace a circular arc.",
            "Velocities map to coordinates in 2D.",
            "Geometry explains why Pi appears here."
        ]

        # Phase space setup

        dot = Dot(color=WHITE)

        # Visual elements
        marker = Circle(radius=0.1, color=WHITE, fill_opacity=1)
        marker.move_to(arc.get_end())
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.play(Create(arc))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.play(FadeIn(dot))
        self.play(MoveAlongPath(dot, arc), run_time=2, rate_func=linear)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(RED)
        self.play(Create(marker))
        self.wait(2)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Pi defines rotation and circular motion.",
            "Constrained systems inherently produce Pi.",
            "Our collisions are simply rotating in space.",
            "Data from collisions forms a perfect circle.",
            "Pi is fundamental to all oscillatory motion."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Conclusion: Why Pi Appears Everywhere", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display the relation N = 10^k * Pi.
        eq1 = MathTex(r"N", r"=", r"10^k", r"\pi")
        eq1.set_color_by_tex(r"N", YELLOW)
        self.place_at_grid(eq1, "B2", scale_factor=1.2)
        self.play(FadeIn(eq1))
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(YELLOW))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Show the scaling factor sqrt(m1/m2) clearly in green #00FF00.
        eq2 = MathTex(r"\sqrt{\frac{m_1}{m_2}}")
        eq2.set_color("#00FF00")
        self.place_at_grid(eq2, "C4", scale_factor=1.2)
        self.play(Write(eq2))
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Data from collisions forms a perfect circle.
        circle = Circle(radius=0.5, color=RED)
        self.place_at_grid(circle, "E3", scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(Create(circle))
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(RED))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # Pi is fundamental to all oscillatory motion.
        final_pi = Tex(r"$\pi$", font_size=72, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(final_pi, "D5", scale_factor=2.0)
        self.play(FadeIn(final_pi))
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Elastic Collision Paradox: Counting Pi with Colliding Blocks
outline.target_audience: High school students with an interest in physics and computer science

sections.title: The Setup: A Curious Mechanical System
sections.content: Introduce the physical system: two blocks of different masses on a frictionless surface, with a wall to the left. The smaller block is placed between the wall and the larger block. All collisions are perfectly elastic.
sections.example: A small toy mouse (mass 1kg) sits between a wall and a heavy elephant (mass 100kg). As the elephant slides toward the mouse, they begin a series of high-speed 'ping-pong' collisions.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Briefly explain that in elastic collisions, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. Visualize this using vector arrows (momentum) and energy bars to show how the blocks trade velocities.
sections.example: Show a visual animation where the 'speed bars' change length exactly according to the mass ratios when they hit, ensuring total energy remains constant.

sections.title: The Mathematical Mapping: Collision Count as Digits
sections.content: Reveal the core discovery: If the mass of the large block is 100^n kg, the total number of collisions between the blocks and the wall will yield the first (n+1) digits of Pi.
sections.example: Show a counter on screen: When mass ratio is 1:1, total collisions = 3. When 1:100, collisions = 31. When 1:10,000, collisions = 314.

sections.title: Visualizing the 'Phase Space' Geometry
sections.content: Explain that the collisions aren't magic; they are geometry. By mapping the velocities as coordinates on a 2D plane, the path of the blocks traces a circular arc that hits a 'barrier' at specific intervals.
sections.example: A graphical representation of a bouncing ball in a circular 'wedge' sector, where the angle of the wedge is determined by the ratio of the square roots of the masses.

sections.title: Conclusion: Why Pi Appears Everywhere
sections.content: Summarize that Pi is a fundamental constant of rotation and circles, which inherently appear whenever we calculate repeated oscillations or collisions in constrained space.
sections.example: A final fast-paced animation showing a 1:1,000,000 ratio block system rapidly clicking 3,141 times, concluding with the image of a circle appearing from the data.
